paper.title: SOCIAL LEARNING THEORY AND CRIMINAL OFFENDING: SOURCES, MECHANISMS AND CONTEMPORARY EXPRESSIONS IN SELECTED EUROPEAN UNION MEMBER STATES
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement, and no DST project reference. …

sample.universe: Peer-reviewed research and official publications on criminal learning available through 23 August 2026 — including reports of Europol, the Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention (Brå), the Bulgarian National Statistical Institute, the European Union Drugs Agency and the Council of Europe — together with five purposively selected EU Member States (Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Italy, Bulgaria) treated as case studies.
sample.unit_of_observation: published study or official report; and country case
selection_rules: structured narrative review covering foundational theory, empirical tests, network research, cybercrime studies and intervention evidence (p.3)
sources restricted to peer-reviewed research and official publications available through 23 August 2026 (p.3)
five Member States selected because each offers evidence about a different transmission setting, not to rank national crime levels (p.3)

Sweden: age-graded network recruitment and digital status signalling; Denmark: register-based evidence on prison peer effects; the Netherlands: cyber-dependent offending with intergenerational organised crime; Italy: mafia-related kinship and territorial socialisation; Bulgaria: administrative data on juvenile offending and educational measures (p.3)

construction_notes: NO ORIGINAL DATA. The article is a structured narrative review combined with a functional comparative case study: "The study uses a structured narrative review and a functional comparative case-study design" (p.1) and "The approach is explanatory rather than statistical" (p.3). It constructs no variables, estimates no model and reports no coefficient, standard error, confidence interval or p-value anywhere.

NO DANISH REGISTER DATA IS USED BY THE AUTHORS. `registers` is deliberately empty. Danish register evidence appears only as a citation: "Damm and Gorinas used register data covering the Danish prison population to examine whether exposure to peers affected crime- specific recidivism" (p.9), footnoted to Damm, A.P. and Gorinas, C., 2020, 'Prison as a criminal school: Peer effects and criminal learning behind bars', Journal of Law and Economics, 63(1), pp. 149-180. The article names no register, no register code and no register variable, and gives no sample size, period or linkage for those data.

This paper appears to be a false positive for a Danish-register economics corpus: it is a criminology/law review article whose only connection to Danish register data is the one secondary citation above. This is consistent with the empty regression digest supplied with this pack (0 regressions, 0 tables, 0 figures).

Table 1, "Functional comparison of criminal learning environments in selected EU Member States" (pp.8-9), is the article's only table. It is a qualitative four-column matrix (Member State and setting / Evidence examined / Principal learning mechanism / Prevention implication) and contains no estimates.

The only numbers printed in the article are counts quoted from other sources, not results: Europol's 821 high-risk criminal networks and more than 25,000 members (p.6); 28 interviewees in the Brå network study (p.8); 1,240 Dutch young people in the Bekkers et al. cyber-offending study (p.10); 25 organised-crime offenders and 48 adult children in the van Dijk et al. study (p.10); seven criminal families in the Spapens and Moors study (p.10); and Bulgarian administrative counts for 2025 — 7,892 minors and juveniles in child pedagogical rooms including 2,385 new entrants, 4,741 crimes, and 6,890 educational measures imposed on 4,840 persons (p.12). The article explicitly states of the last of these that "These figures describe administrative activity and recorded behaviour; they cannot establish differential association, imitation or reinforcement" (p.12), so they are not recorded as claims.

PROVENANCE OF BIBLIOGRAPHIC FIELDS: neither the publication year nor the journal name is printed in the article body. `year` = 2026 is inferred from the PDF creation date (2026-09-09), from sources being cited 'available through 23 August 2026', and from references dated 2026; `journal` is taken from the PDF metadata fields /Subject ('Scientific article prepared for E-Journal VFU') and /Comments ('Formatted to the technical requirements of E-Journal VFU'). The printed page range is 542-559. No DOI is printed.
PAGE NUMBERS in every quote and evidence record refer to PDF page indices (1-18), not the printed journal page numbers (542-559). PDF page n corresponds to printed page 541+n.

claims.statement: Differential association — patterned exposure to people, messages and criminal opportunities differing in frequency, duration, priority and intensity — is one of the two components of social learning theory most consistently supported as a source of criminal offending in the reviewed European evidence.

definition.value: Patterned exposure to people, messages and opportunities, not mere physical proximity to an offender; associations differ in frequency, duration, priority and intensity, and transmit techniques, motives, rationalisations and attitudes while also structuring criminal opportunity. Assessed qualitatively across the reviewed studies and country cases.

Criminal conduct in general — its acquisition, maintenance, escalation and abandonment. The article treats offending as a qualitative outcome assessed across reviewed studies and official reports; it constructs no offending variable of its own.

magnitude.interpretation: "the strongest support" (abstract); "the most consistently visible components" together with definitions (section 6). No quantitative magnitude is given.

estimand.target_population: Not an estimate for a defined population: a qualitative assessment of how strongly the reviewed European evidence supports this component of social learning theory.

population.description: Offenders, prisoners and young people as described in the peer-reviewed research and official publications reviewed, for five purposively selected EU Member States (Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Italy, Bulgaria).

identification.source_of_variation: None. The article analyses no data of its own: it combines a structured narrative review of published research and official publications with a functional comparative case study of five EU Member States. There is no reform, lottery, discontinuity, instrument or other exogenous variation, and the authors describe the approach as explanatory rather than statistical.

key_assumptions.assumption: Functional comparability: the five purposively selected country cases each isolate a setting in which the theory makes a distinct prediction, and the comparison asks only whether the observed recruitment, transmission and reinforcement processes correspond to theory-predicted mechanisms rather than ranking national crime levels.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicit statement of the comparative logic and its limits in section 2 (methodology)

key_assumptions.assumption: Convergent validity of heterogeneous secondary sources: findings drawn from self-report studies and from official reports designed for administration or threat assessment rather than for testing criminological theory are treated as convergent evidence and interpreted cautiously.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the authors state the two limitations and say findings are treated as convergent evidence and interpreted cautiously

key_assumptions.assumption: Self-selection into peer groups is conceded and not resolved: an unobserved pre-existing criminal propensity drives both whom a person associates with and whether they offend, so observed peer similarity is partly cause and partly consequence.
key_assumptions.supported_by: conceded as the first of four limitations preventing a monocausal conclusion; no design or test is offered against it

key_assumptions.assumption: Measurement: much social-learning research relies on self-reported delinquency and on respondents' descriptions of their friends, which can inflate apparent similarity through projection.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as a limitation in both the methodology section and the critical assessment

key_assumptions.assumption: Causation between association and offending is reciprocal rather than one-directional, so the relationship cannot be read as a single directed effect; the article states an inference rather than a causal conclusion where the evidence is descriptive.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated in section 3.1 and reaffirmed in the methodology; no attempt to separate the directions

projection and measurement error in self-reported peer delinquency
limited scope: spontaneous, expressive or highly impulsive offending may involve little transmitted technique
structural omission: the theory explains transmission better than exposure to criminal models
non-comparability of national administrative categories, age thresholds and reporting practices

estimator.value: None — structured narrative review combined with a functional comparative case study; no statistical model is estimated and no coefficient is reported.

source_table.value: No regression table or figure. Qualitative assessment stated in the abstract (p.1) and section 6, "Critical assessment: explanatory strength and limits" (p.13); the only table, Table 1 (pp.8-9), is a qualitative comparison matrix.

heterogeneity.finding: Visible in every case: "Swedish recruits encounter age-proximate models and hierarchical meanings; Dutch criminal families transmit attitudes and opportunity; Italian mafia contexts intensify identity and loyalty; cyber communities connect skill with recognition" (p.13).

heterogeneity.dimension: network structure vs number of delinquent friends
heterogeneity.finding: The article reports Haynie's finding that the peer-delinquency relationship depends partly on the structure and composition of friendship networks, not only on the number of delinquent friends (p.4).
Association matters most where offending requires repeated interaction, specialised knowledge or group reinforcement, and least for isolated or highly impulsive offending (p.13).

ambiguities: The article reports no coefficient, standard error or test statistic for this or any relationship, so the claim records only an asserted direction and the authors' qualitative strength ranking ("strongest support").
The authors concede that selection and reciprocal causation are unresolved, so the asserted direction is not separated from reverse causation or common-cause selection.
The paper's own evidential basis for this proposition is a review of other authors' studies plus five country cases; it performs no original estimation.

heterogeneity.finding: Dutch criminal families transmit attitudes and opportunity and Italian mafia contexts intensify identity and loyalty; in Calabria the article reports socio-cultural transmission of mafia behaviour through family bonds, loyalty, silence and role expectations (pp.11-13).

Within a criminal group informal rules may compete with state law and carry more immediate social consequences, so a young recruit may fear ridicule, exclusion or retaliation more than a remote probability of formal punishment (p.5).

The article stresses the symmetry: pro-social definitions can be learned, reinforced and stabilised through the same process, so the theory explains conformity and desistance as well as crime (pp.5, 13).

claims.statement: Evidence that imitation of criminal models produces criminal offending is more context-dependent than evidence on association and definitions: imitation alone is rarely sufficient for complex crime, because capability, access and trust determine whether observed conduct becomes executable.

definition.value: Observational learning from a criminal model: the prospective offender observes a model, retains a script, assesses whether the behaviour appears competent or rewarded, and attempts reproduction. The model need not be physically present — videos, encrypted chats, livestreams and forum tutorials can demonstrate weapons, fraud techniques, hacking tools or ideological violence. Assessed qualitatively across the reviewed studies.

claims.statement: Digital platforms accelerate exposure to criminal models, their visibility and vicarious reward, but they rarely operate independently of offline relationships and opportunities and should not be treated as an autonomous cause of offending.

definition.value: Digital environments that reduce the cost of finding like-minded peers, preserve instructional material, display successful models and generate visible reinforcement through attention, status metrics and group approval — including videos, encrypted chats, livestreams and forum tutorials. Assessed qualitatively across the reviewed studies and country cases.

The scale and speed of criminal social learning: the frequency of exposure to criminal models, the apparent consensus and visibility of criminal conduct, and vicarious reward through attention, status metrics and group approval. Treated by the article as the intermediate product of digital association rather than as offending itself.
